newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Dini rejects government "Euro-tax" change.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Dini rejects government "Euro-tax" change.

text.p: Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini rejected the centre-left government's proposed changes to its controversial "Euro-tax" as "completely insufficient".

The government submitted the change late on Wednesday after Dini's small centrist party, Italian Renewal, outlined alternative measures to raise 12.5 trillion lire ($8.3 billion) planned by Prime Minister Romano Prodi to help get Italy in shape to be a founder member of Europe's single currency.
"We judge the government amendment to be completely insufficient," Dini told reporters late on Wednesday. "It does not meet any of our requests."
His party is a member of Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left coalition government.
The government proposal would raise the tax threshold for the self-employed to 15.2 million lire from 10 million lire but left a proposed threshold for employees unchanged at 23 million.
It also outlined various tax deductions.
Italian Renewal had earlier presented proposals including imposing a corporate tax instead of a planned levy on severance pay and a one-off charge on early retirement pensions.

Foreign Trade Minister Augusto Fantozzi, a member of Dini's party, said in an interview with La Stampa that Italian Renewal was not intending to sabotage the Euro-tax, a key element in the 1997 budget.

"We're not making any ultimatum, but the Euro-tax can be improved," Fantozzi said. "We want to improve a measure that can and should be improved...It is important that such an important measure should have the widest consensus possible."
Prodi's 1997 budget aims to slash 62.5 trillion lire off next year's projected deficit.
